title: Tell me about this record
editorialContent:
# Meir Schreibman and the Community Elections in Sokółka

## What the memorial-book record says

The record for [Meir Schreibman](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_0d8947f4709aeb22a7909848) is brief but places him in a significant moment of Jewish communal and political life. The memorial book identifies him as one of the leaders of the **Nonpartisan Workers Party** list during preparations for elections to the Jewish community council. In the original Hebrew/Yiddish-script evidence, his name appears as מאיר שרייבמאן. The supplied scan identifies him by name, while the surrounding translated passage gives the fuller political context.

The memorial book describes [Preparations for community elections](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_867a9821e19ab969ff6aec8f) among the Jews of [the Sokolka Jewish community](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_b4937d55a4d4d00439c03624). According to the account, after the German conquest during the First World War, Jewish communal and cultural life revived. Various political, educational, cultural, and religious groups were founded or re-established, and these groups began organizing lists for elections to the community council. The JewishGen translation of the relevant section names Meir Schreibman—rendered there as “Meyer Schreiberman”—alongside Meyer Yulewitz as a head of the “Non-Aligned Workers’ Party” list. [Memorial Book of Sokolka, pages 123–151](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html) records that the two men spoke at an election meeting in the old synagogue and urged voters to support list number 10. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html))

This means that Meir was not merely a passive candidate. The account presents him as a public speaker and political representative who addressed voters directly. It does not, however, provide his age, occupation, family relationships, residence, later fate, or a fuller biography. Those absences are important: the evidence allows us to identify his political role in this particular election campaign, but not to reconstruct his entire life with confidence.

## A crowded political field

Meir Schreibman’s party operated within a highly pluralistic Jewish political environment. The memorial book lists [Young Zionists](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_1a82db37302ec15cc535c14d), [The Center](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_39f35139067bfbf4cdde713c), [Kadima](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_70e53441716a19794898cef4), [Flowers of Zion](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_a524c419def09d2b00a84637), [Herut and Revival](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_2d4814750c1bf54402643064), and [The Bund](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_9ed2af16fb59efa677430fcd) among the organizations active or represented in Sokółka. These names reflect several different visions of Jewish communal life: Zionist nationalism, religious traditionalism, Jewish labor politics, and secular or socialist culture.

The memorial book characterizes the Bund as the only explicitly anti-Zionist party in the local political contest. It describes the Zionists as the dominant force, while also noting the importance of traditionalist Jews and religious workers. The Nonpartisan Workers Party emerged in opposition to the Bund, but it was not simply identical with the mainstream Zionist parties. Its name suggests an attempt to appeal to Jewish workers without formally aligning with one of the established ideological camps. The available record does not explain the party’s program in detail, so it would be unsafe to assign it a precise ideological position beyond its documented opposition to the Bund and its appeal to workers.

The surrounding campaign was energetic and sometimes theatrical. According to the memorial-book account, meetings were held both in synagogues and outdoors; candidates made speeches, promises, and mutual accusations; and party numbers were displayed throughout the town. The Zionists were associated with number 6, the Bund with number 5, and Meir Schreibman’s list with number 10. The narrative even recalls campaign posters being placed on animals led through the streets, an anecdote that conveys how thoroughly the election entered everyday communal life. [The JewishGen translation of the election chapter](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html) presents this episode as part of a broader struggle over the direction of the “Jewish street”—including education, charitable assistance, and communal administration. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html))

## Sokółka’s Jewish community as the setting

The political activity associated with Meir Schreibman took place in a community with deep institutional roots. The Virtual Shtetl history of Sokółka states that Jews were present in the town by the second half of the seventeenth century and that communal privileges were confirmed in 1698. By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Jewish life centered on the market, trade, crafts, synagogues, religious schools, a mikveh, charitable structures, and educational institutions. The town had several synagogues and a Jewish quarter containing the main synagogue, houses of prayer, and communal buildings. [Virtual Shtetl’s history of Sokółka](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community) describes Jews as central to local commerce and artisan production, including ownership of most of the town’s shops in the late 1930s. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community))

The same source emphasizes that Jewish political life expanded after Poland regained independence in 1918. It records branches of major Jewish parties, active Zionist circles, youth organizations, and substantial Jewish participation in elections. In the 1927 municipal election, Jewish candidates won 14 of 24 seats on the Municipal Board, and one became vice-mayor. This wider pattern helps explain why a community-council election could attract such intense attention: communal institutions governed education, welfare, religious services, and access to outside assistance, while political parties represented competing visions of Jewish collective life. [Virtual Shtetl’s account of Sokółka](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community) provides this broader civic and institutional context. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community))

![Sokółka Jewish quarter and historic town context](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2c/Unpaved_steet_in_the_Frysztak_Ghetto.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Jewish_ghettos_in_German-occupied_Poland")

## Meir’s associates and political significance

The memorial-book evidence links Meir most directly with Meyer Yulewitz, who appears beside him as a leader and speaker for the Nonpartisan Workers Party list. It also places him in opposition to the Bund and within a broader field shaped by Zionist and traditionalist organizations. The record does not establish kinship between Meir and any of these people or organizations; the connections are political and communal rather than necessarily familial.

The election account also shows that Jewish political divisions were not abstract. They concerned who would control practical resources and communal priorities. The memorial book says that the community council would influence American aid, education, and the administration of Jewish communal affairs. The Bund emphasized secular education and workers’ interests; Zionists emphasized Jewish nationalism and the Land of Israel; religious factions defended traditional observance. Meir’s role therefore belongs to a debate over how Jewish communal autonomy should be organized, not merely to a contest over party labels.

The later history of Sokółka gives this political activity a tragic retrospective meaning. During the German occupation beginning in 1941, the Jewish population was confined in a ghetto, and Jews from Sokółka and surrounding towns were subjected to forced labor. The Virtual Shtetl account states that the ghetto existed until January 24, 1943, and that most of Sokółka’s Jewish inhabitants were murdered at Treblinka. [Virtual Shtetl’s history of the Sokółka community](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community) records this destruction, while its separate account of the [Sokółka ghetto](https://sztetl.org.pl/pl/miejscowosci/s/852-sokolka/116-miejsca-martyrologii/50937-getto-w-sokolce) describes the ghetto’s liquidation and deportations. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community)) ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/pl/miejscowosci/s/852-sokolka/116-miejsca-martyrologii/50937-getto-w-sokolce?utm_source=openai))

Nothing in the supplied record confirms what happened to Meir Schreibman personally. His appearance in the election narrative preserves one moment in which he acted publicly on behalf of a workers’ political list. Beyond that, his fate must remain unidentified unless further records—such as survivor testimony, postwar memorial lists, archival documents, or genealogical records—can be located. The name variation “Meir Schreibman” / “Meyer Schreiberman” may reflect transliteration and translation practices, but the available evidence does not by itself prove whether every occurrence of the variant refers to the same individual.
